title: tk herd collect boundary check conflates tracker state with project config
description:
Found live on tick sqt (2026-08-19). collect reported boundary-violation for .tick/config.md and .tick/runners.toml on a tick whose ENTIRE PURPOSE was to migrate those two files. The orchestrator had to hand-verify that no tracker state was touched before merging.

The boundary invariant is that IMPLEMENTERS NEVER MUTATE TRACKER STATE — the orchestrator owns tick status, notes and the activity log. But .tick/ holds two different kinds of thing:
- TRACKER STATE, orchestrator-owned: .tick/issues/*.json, .tick/activity/*.jsonl, .tick/logs/
- PROJECT CONFIG AND CONTENT, ordinary repo files a tick may legitimately change: config.md, runners.toml, learnings.md

Treating the whole directory as orchestrator-owned means any tick that legitimately edits project config trips a violation, and the operator learns to wave the check through — which is exactly how a real breach gets merged one day.

Fix: scope the check to tracker state (.tick/issues, .tick/activity, .tick/logs) rather than all of .tick/. Config files stay reviewable through the normal diff. If a repo wants config edits flagged, make that a distinct, softer signal — a note in the report, not the same verdict as mutating tick status.

Companion gap worth considering in the same tick: collect has no notion of workspace hygiene. sqt also created a herdr workspace in the operator UI (wAT) that nothing would have caught; the orchestrator only found it because the operator saw it appear. A collect that reported run-created workspaces outside the tick manifest would close a leak the substrate currently has no policy layer for.
acceptance_criteria: A tick that edits .tick/config.md or .tick/runners.toml and no tracker state collects as ready-to-merge; a tick that edits .tick/issues or .tick/activity still reports boundary-violation naming the files; the distinction is covered by tests.
